newsitem.title: USA: S&P affirms Province of Ontario, Ontario Hydro.
newsitem.headline: S&P affirms Province of Ontario, Ontario Hydro.

text.p: Standard & Poor's today has affirmed its double-A'-minus long-term debt rating and its A-1'-plus short-term rating on the Province of Ontario.
Also, Standard & Poor's has affirmed its double-A'-minus long-term and A-1'-plus short-term debt ratings of Ontario Hydro, guaranteed by the province.
The outlook remains stable.
The ratings reflect:

-- The government's commitment to further reduction of the province's still-large fiscal deficit, despite the revenue pressures associated with its simultaneous focus on reducing personal tax rates; and
-- A strong and diverse economic base, with expectations of continued export growth and improving domestic demand through the medium term.
Deficit projections for fiscal 1998, as well as 1997 results, were in line with expectations based upon last year's medium-term plan.

This year's anticipated second phase of personal income tax cuts, combined with ongoing federal transfer reductions, are offset only in part by projections for robust corporations and sales taxes, and gaming revenues.
Total revenue in 1998 will fall by 1.5%, following a 0.7% decline in 1997.
Total spending will fall by 5.0% in 1998. In 1997, spending was down 2.7%, though over budget due to much greater-than-anticipated restructuring costs.

These one-time charges included not only the severance costs of staffing reductions, but also renovation, equipment, and retraining costs related to institutional reforms, particularly in health care.
The deficit declined according to plan, to 16% of revenue in 1997 from 19% in 1996.
It is projected to be 12% in 1998, still high compared with other Standard & Poor's-rated regional governments globally.

Economic expansion slowed to a 2.0% annual rate in 1996, reflecting the several months of consumer caution and higher interest rates that followed the October 1995 Quebec referendum, and continued high (9.1%) unemployment.

The province projects more robust and broader-based growth of 3.2% in 1997, as consumer demand and residential construction respond to lower interest rates, and business investment and exports remain strong.
Employment growth of 2% should force the unemployment rate to decline, though only gradually. Planned GDP growth in the 3% area underpins revenue targets through 1999.
The government is committed to meeting its deficit goals even if economic performance, and revenues, fall short of plan.

Due to high deficits and slow deficit reduction, net tax-supported debt has increased throughout a period of slow but steady economic growth, to an estimated 32% of GDP in fiscal 1997 from 25% in 1993, though debt should plateau at about 34% in 1998.
Provincial debt-to-revenues will reach 220% in 1998, the highest among Canadian provinces.
Improving fiscal performance, as the province advances towards a zero deficit by 2001, is expected to moderate the debt burden beyond 1998.
OUTLOOK: Stable.
The outlook anticipates the government's willingness to rapidly adjust spending further should this prove necessary to meet its zero-deficit target.
The outlook also reflects the expectation of good economic performance over the medium term, Standard & Poor's said.
